mentions.text: Agreed, I've been saying essentially the same thing for years. GP pointed out that Coca-Cola can't ban you from buying their product in practice, but I would argue that moreover they shouldn't be able to ban you in principle even if they somehow could. Past a certain scale, or at least past a certain scale and longevity, goods and services become de facto public infrastructure and should be treated as such. I'm all for freedoms of speech, association, and enterprise, but I also appreciate ideas like right to internet access / freedom to connect[1], and in hindsight I would argue that freedom to connect is just a specific case of a more general principle of freedom to consume the same goods and services as the broader public. It's like, Mocha Joe banning you from his coffee shop is a minor nuisance, but finding out that you're never allowed to enter any Starbucks in the world in perpetuity would be somewhat life-altering. An algorithm at Apple or Google deciding it doesn't like the cut of your jib, much more so. mentions.text: My parents live in a different Northern Virginia suburb that has a lot of gleaming mixed use developments filled with private equity owned chains (Tatte, Sweetgreen and the like). Tucked away is this semi-industrial plaza that is falling apart and filled with small independent local businesses. I think it's the last little patch of that town with cheap rent, so it's a hub for entrepreneurship. Enatye is the best ethiopian food I've ever had, local chains Weird Brothers Coffee and Aslin both started back there, and there's a cute little French cafe with lovely sandwiches. Those massive new mixed use plazas by metro stations have sky high rent and a small local business can never afford it, so those are filled with Starbucks and Sweetgreen. I think this is a lot of what the author of this post is getting at. Urbanism so often means gleaming expensive sterile mixed use developments, when what makes places so special are these areas where people really can start their own businesses.

mentions.text: 100% agree that the end result is nowhere near as good. At the same time, I think Nespresso is a fascinating lesson in prioritization. Nespresso gives you: (1) an inexpensive entry point, even if in the long run capsules are often more expensive than beans, (2) a taste that's "good enough" for many people who like coffee, even those who sneer at Starbucks, and (3) perhaps most importantly, perfect consistency without any time nor effort. Once you find a capsule you like, you can produce that same tasting coffee without having to think about adjusting your grind to your beans as they age, or whether you've perfected your tamping technique. A friend has an Olympia Express, a classic lever espresso machine that makes truly great coffee, and a high-end grinder to match. He also has a Nespresso machine, because his wife has no interest in dealing with a grinder or learning how to use the lever to get her coffee, especially when trying to get their kid to school in the morning. They both end up drinking Nespresso during the week, and the Olympia mostly gets used on weekends. Even for people who love good coffee, Nespresso is often still a reasonable tradeoff.

mentions.text: It's really not though. I only get to vote for my representatives. If the entire federal government is doing something that's a problem or even a specific federal agency, I have no ability to just stop. If we see massive fraud happening from a charity using our donations, I can personally stop giving that charity my money. If I don't like how Starbucks sources its ingredients or treats its employees, I can go to another local coffee shop. Even at the local level, if I don't like how my city, county or state government operates...I can move and many people do. At the Federal level, we're all stuck with it especially to the degree that most agencies continue with virtually no changes from leadership changes with congressional deadlocks. It's the sole reason we have $40 trillion in debt, because none of us can just stop giving the money.

mentions.text: The difference is actually small. By default a cup at Starbucks is much more volume than a default Nespresso capsule, like 2-3 capsules, so you can't compare 1 Starbucks cup with 1 capsule. Then the main thing that makes Starbucks "worse" is energy to operate the store, assuming it'd close down if everyone would use a Nespresso instead in the home/office. And if you're in California in the summer and all that energy is effectively renewable, that difference too disappears. At that point they're very comparable. As for the cups ie. containers, one takeaway cup vs 2-3 capsules are pretty similar. If you ignore the store part then Nespresso was never meaningfully better. And if you put (cow) milk in your coffee, that dominates anyway so the above can be ignored. But really just don't use either. Go to a local coffee place and use generic brand capsule machines. Starbucks coffee is crap, if local coffee places are more expensive (which is rare) you might as well get coffee from McD's or 7/11, it isn't any worse. If you just want sugary dopamine, not judging but then we're no longer talking coffee.

mentions.text: Awhile back, a local Starbucks was doing some sort of "blind taste-test" challenge, and I had no problem differentiating between the instant, the pod, and the brewed coffee. Flavor profiles are just completely different between the three. And I'm not exactly a coffee snob -- if gas station coffee is what's available, I'm grateful for the gas station coffee. Cowboy Coffee has to be my favorite brew -- pot of water at a rolling boil, toss in ground coffee, let it boil. The rolling boil does a great job of outgassing while keeping everything piping hot, by far the smoothest cup I've had across every method I've tried. Downside is it sucks to clean, and you're going to get a bit of mud at the bottom of the cup, so I just stick with a filter machine most of the time: it's Good Enough, especially if you use a decent ground coffee and don't skimp on the quantity. People today don't know how much a revolution homemade filter coffee was back in the mid-70s, it was a big deal to have a "professional" coffee machine at home -- the kind you would see at a restaurant -- back when the standard home method was the percolator.
